how-much-to-charge.html.text:
← Snow removal bid calculator

How much should I charge for snow removal?

A $350 seasonal driveway contract that looks comfortable at eight storms a winter is often underwater at fourteen — especially once "ice included" turns out to mean unlimited ice events at no extra charge. Snow removal is priced on the route and the winter you expect, not on one driveway on one good day.

Open the free snow removal bid calculator

What a flat seasonal price cannot see

Storm count. Eight storms and fourteen storms are different winters. A seasonal price that only pencils out at the low end is a bet you're taking on the weather.

Ice events. Ice knockdown is its own labor and material cost. "Ice included" without a limit means every ice event that winter comes out of the same flat price.

Trigger depth. A 1-inch trigger fires far more often than a 2-inch trigger in many Northeast and Midwest metros. Route minutes at a low trigger depth over a real winter, not a national average, are what the price should be built from.

A bid you can defend

  1. Time each stop — plow, sidewalk, and drive time — and price it at a loaded operator-and-truck hourly.
  2. Add salt as its own cost per application.
  3. Multiply by the storm count and ice-event count you actually expect for the season, using your own trigger depth and recent winters.
  4. Price the seasonal so margin is a share of the whole winter, not a markup on one driveway.

The calculator does that arithmetic in your browser. It does not forecast weather — it prices the storm and ice-event count you enter, and reports the break-even storm count for a proposed seasonal price.

Worked example

A $350 seasonal driveway contract priced against an assumed eight storms and no ice events can look like healthy margin. Run the same route minutes and loaded hourly against fourteen storms and a handful of ice events — a realistic winter in many Northeast and Midwest metros with a 1-inch trigger — and the same $350 price can be underwater before the season ends. The calculator reports the break-even storm count so that number is known before the contract is signed, not discovered in February.

Common questions

How do I price a snow removal contract?

Time each stop (plow + sidewalk + drive time), price those minutes at a loaded operator-and-truck hourly, add salt, then multiply by the storms and ice events you actually expect. Margin is a share of the seasonal price, not a markup on one driveway.

Is a seasonal snow removal contract better than per push?

Seasonal is only better for the contractor if the quote covers a long winter plus ice events. A $350 driveway seasonal that looked fine at eight storms often loses money at fourteen, especially with unlimited ice.

How many snow events should I estimate?

Use your own trigger depth and last few winters, not a national average. In many Northeast and Midwest metros a 1-inch trigger fires more often than a 2-inch trigger. This tool does not forecast weather — it prices the event count you enter.

No warranty. This free page is not legal, tax, financial, engineering, or business advice, and it does not tell you what to charge. It is not a weather forecast and it does not replace a qualified professional. Verify every figure against your own payroll, insurance, fuel, and material costs before relying on it or submitting a bid. FOR SNOW-REMOVAL CONTRACTORS

Price the winter, not the driveway.

A $350 seasonal that looked fine at eight storms is often underwater at fourteen — especially if ice is “included.” This calculator prices a route from minutes on site, deadhead, a loaded truck, salt, and the event count you actually expect. You get a per-push price, a seasonal, the ice drain, and the storm count where a cheap quote dies.

How much should I charge for snow removal?

The route

One row per stop. Minutes are a starting point — time your own truck and replace them. Ice minutes default to 65% of plow + sidewalk (salt and walks, not a full push) and stay editable.

Site typePlow minWalk minSalt bagsIce minIce bags

Your costs

A long storm on a 4-hour route is often two passes. Set passes to 1.3 or 2 if you typically re-hit the route before it ends. Payroll burden is employer taxes, workers’ compensation, and paid time off — the part that never shows up on the wage.

The winter you are bidding

Use your trigger depth and your last few winters, not a national average. A 1-inch trigger fires more often than a 2-inch trigger. This is not a weather forecast.

Questions contractors actually ask

How do I price a snow removal contract?

Time each stop, price those minutes at a loaded operator-and-truck hourly, add salt, then multiply by the storms and ice events you expect. Do not start from a neighbor’s driveway price.

Per push or seasonal?

Offer both. Seasonal only works if the quote survives a long winter plus ice. Paste a number you are considering and the tool will say how many storms it can absorb.

What about unlimited ice?

Ice is usually salt and sidewalks, not a full plow — and there are often more ice events than snow events. Price them as their own line or the “included” clause eats the season.

vs-a-flat-seasonal-rate.html.text:
← Snow Removal Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. quoting one flat seasonal rate for every driveway

Setting one seasonal number from last year's memory and quoting it to every stop on the route is the fastest way to price a winter. It is also the fastest way to lose money on the one stop that doesn't look like the others, or the one winter that runs heavier than you guessed. This calculator prices each stop from its own minutes and salt, and reports the storm count any number you're already considering actually survives.

What each approach actually does

A flat seasonal rate is a number set once, usually from how a typical driveway priced out last winter, and then quoted to every new stop regardless of its size, sidewalk length, or salt use. It takes seconds to quote and needs no math on the phone. What it cannot do is tell you whether that number still clears a margin on a stop that isn't a typical driveway, or on a winter that isn't a typical winter.

This calculator prices each stop from its own plow minutes, sidewalk minutes, and salt bags, with ice events priced as their own line rather than folded into a plow visit, against a loaded operator-and-truck hourly, payroll burden, salt cost, overhead, and target margin. Enter a seasonal number you're already considering and it reports the profit, the margin, and the storm count that number breaks even at — on that specific stop, at the storm count you actually expect, not a number recalled from a different route in a different winter.

QuestionWhere to answer it
What should I charge this specific stop, given its own minutes and salt?This calculator — free, instant, private, no account.
Does the flat number I already quote hold up on a bigger or smaller stop?This calculator's proposed-price check, run against that stop's own sites.
How many storms can the seasonal I'm already charging actually survive?This calculator's break-even storm count.
I just need a number to say out loud on the phone right now.A flat rate — faster, and fine for a route of near-identical stops in a market you already know cold.
How does the math behind a snow-removal seasonal actually work?This calculator's own pricing walkthrough.

The same $950 flat quote, three stops, one storm count

Using this calculator's own shipped defaults — a $22/hr loaded operator plus a $45/hr truck, 30% payroll burden, $8/bag salt, 15% overhead, a 20% target margin, 10 expected snow events and 6 ice events — and a $950 flat seasonal quoted to three different stops:

StopTrue seasonal costProfit at $950 flatMargin
Two-car driveway$764.95$185.0519.5%
Sidewalks / walkways only$725.05$224.9523.7%
Medium commercial lot (20–50 cars)$2,871.96−$1,921.96−202.3%

The $950 quote clears a healthy margin on the two stops it happens to resemble, and loses $1,921.96 the moment it's quoted to the commercial lot — whose own ice-and-plow cost, $2,871.96, is already three times the flat number before a dollar of profit. Nothing about the arithmetic changed between stops; only the stop's own minutes and salt did, and a number set from memory has no field for that.

The same driveway, three winters

Hold the stop fixed — the two-car driveway above — and the same $950 flat quote, and vary only the storm count:

Snow eventsTrue seasonal costProfit at $950 flatMargin
8 (a mild winter)$663.99$286.0130.1%
10 (the planned case)$764.95$185.0519.5%
14 (a heavy winter)$966.86−$16.86−1.8%

Nothing about the driveway changed between rows — only the storm count did. A flat $950 set from a mild, 8-event winter looks generous the next year at 10 events, and quietly goes underwater at 14: the exact shape the calculator's own break-even figure exists to catch before the season, not after it.

All figures recomputed live from calc.mjs, the same arithmetic the calculator itself runs — not typed once and left to drift.

Common questions

Why not just quote one flat seasonal number and move on?

Because the number that clears a healthy margin on one stop can already be underwater on another, and the flat quote has no way to tell you which. On this calculator's own defaults (a $22/hr loaded operator plus a $45/hr truck, 30% payroll burden, $8/bag salt, 15% overhead, a 20% target margin, 10 expected snow events and 6 ice events), a $950 flat seasonal clears $185.05 profit at 19.5% margin on a two-car driveway. Quote that same $950 to a medium commercial lot instead, and it loses $1,921.96 — a -202.3% margin — because the lot's own ice-and-plow cost alone is $2,871.96 before a dollar of profit. A flat number quoted from memory cannot see that difference; it was never computed from either stop's minutes or salt.

What happens if the winter turns out heavier than I assumed?

The same flat number that looked fine at the storm count you guessed can go underwater at the storm count you actually get, on the exact same driveway. Take that same two-car driveway and hold the $950 flat quote fixed: at 8 snow events the route's true cost is $663.99, so the flat quote clears $286.01 (30.1% margin); at 10 events, its planned case, cost rises to $764.95 and profit falls to $185.05 (19.5%); at 14 events — the kind of heavier winter a trigger-depth change or a bad season can produce — true cost climbs to $966.86, and the same $950 flat quote loses $16.86. Nothing about the driveway changed; only the storm count did, and a flat number set once from memory has no field for that.

Is picking one flat number ever the right call?

Yes, for a route of near-identical stops in a market with a storm count you already know cold from many seasons of your own records — a flat number set that way is really just this calculator's own math, done once and reused. It stops working the moment the route mixes stop sizes (a two-car driveway next to a commercial lot), or the storm count is uncertain enough that a heavier winter is plausible. This calculator does not know your market's snowfall any better than you do; it turns whatever storm count and stop list you enter into a price, and reports the break-even storm count for any number you're already considering, instead of asking you to hold all of that in your head.

Is my data uploaded anywhere?

No. The calculator runs entirely in your browser. "Copy share link" encodes your stops, rates, and expected winter into this page's own URL hash so a partner or the office can open the same bid — nothing is sent to a server. The optional usage counter records only which features were used, stored locally, and never your route, wages, costs, or prices.

This page names no vendor as a competitor — it compares against the generic method of quoting one flat seasonal number from memory, not a competing calculator or service. vs-aspire.html.text:
← Snow Removal Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. Aspire

Two different shapes: Aspire is an account-based business-management platform for running a landscape or snow company's whole operation. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this winter's route cost, given its stops, minutes, salt, and storm count — before you send the bid.

What each tool is for

Aspire is a cloud business-management platform, founded in 2013 by Kevin Kehoe and Mark Tipton, headquartered in Chesterfield, Missouri. It is built for landscape maintenance and construction, snow and ice management, and commercial cleaning contractors, and has been part of ServiceTitan since ServiceTitan's 2021 acquisition of it. It bundles CRM and lead tracking, estimating, scheduling, purchasing, job costing, mobile crew time tracking, invoicing, and accounting and payroll integration into one ongoing subscription account, with a mobile app for crews in the field. Its own plans are tiered by a contractor's annual revenue rather than sold at one flat price, and no dollar figure for any plan is published on its site — pricing is reached by requesting a demo. Aspire's own pricing page is not reachable from this session to confirm today's exact tier names or any dollar figure, so no price for it is invented here: only its well-documented identity and category — a business-management platform serving landscape, snow and ice, and cleaning contractors, sold as a revenue-tiered subscription account — are stated, and no dollar amount for Aspire appears on this page.

This calculator does none of what Aspire does. It does not track a lead, schedule a crew, or invoice a customer, and it stores no customer or job record on a server. It takes one winter's route — each stop's plow minutes, sidewalk minutes, and salt bags, with ice events priced as their own line at their own minutes and salt rather than folded into a plow visit — plus loaded operator-and-truck hourly, payroll burden, salt cost, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into the per-push price, the seasonal price, the per ice-event price, the walk-away price below which the winter loses money, and how many snow events a seasonal quote actually survives once ice is already paid — plus, if you already have a number on the table, a check of whether it clears that walk-away floor, and a single printable customer proposal for that one winter. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

I run a landscape or snow company and need leads, estimates, scheduling, purchasing, and invoicing tracked in one system across every crew and every season.Aspire, or a comparable business-management platform — running the whole operation is not something this calculator does.

How much does ice control actually add over a seasonal that only priced the plow visits?This calculator's ice-event minutes and salt, priced as their own line, not folded into a plow visit.
How many storms can a seasonal price I'm considering actually survive?This calculator's break-even storm count.
I need my whole crew scheduling, purchasing, and job costing running from one shared account across the season.Aspire — built as an ongoing, account-based platform for exactly that job.
How does the math behind a snow-removal seasonal actually work?This calculator's own pricing walkthrough.
Do I need to create an account or sign up to use the tool?This calculator: no. Aspire is used through a subscription account, and its site describes plans as scaled to a contractor's annual revenue rather than sold to a solo operator at a flat price.

Most snow and landscape companies get different value from each: Aspire (or a comparable platform) for running the company's whole lead-to-invoice operation as an ongoing, revenue-tiered subscription, and a private calculator like this one for an instant, no-login answer to what one winter's route should cost from its stops, minutes, salt, and storm count before a business system is involved. This page's own figures are a pricing model, not a lead record, a scheduled job, or a signed contract.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or Aspire?

They do different jobs, and a snow or landscape company of any size will likely end up touching both eventually. Aspire, founded in 2013 by Kevin Kehoe and Mark Tipton and headquartered in Chesterfield, Missouri, is a cloud business-management platform built for landscape, snow and ice management, and commercial cleaning contractors, and has been part of ServiceTitan since ServiceTitan's 2021 acquisition of it. It bundles CRM and lead tracking, estimating, scheduling, purchasing, job costing, mobile crew time tracking, invoicing, and accounting and payroll integration into one ongoing subscription account, with plans tiered by a contractor's annual revenue rather than one flat price, and no dollar figure published for any plan — you request a demo to get a quote. This calculator does one narrower thing: starting from each stop's plow minutes, sidewalk minutes, and salt bags, with ice events priced as their own line rather than folded into a plow visit, plus loaded operator-and-truck hourly, payroll burden, salt cost, overhead, and target margin, it turns that into the per-push price, the seasonal price, the per ice-event price, the walk-away price below which the winter loses money, and how many storms a seasonal quote actually survives after ice is paid, plus a printable customer proposal for that one winter — before any of it touches a business-management system. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type. A snow or landscape company that already tracks leads, schedules crews, and invoices across a whole season is better served by Aspire or a comparable platform; a contractor who wants an instant, private answer to what one winter's route should cost from its stops, minutes, and storm count before opening a business system is in the right place here.
